Algebra I · Lesson 8.5

Optimization

Solve this lesson →All lessons

Lesson 8.4 ended on a promise. The corners of a region are the points to check when one point must be picked as best. This lesson keeps that promise. Optimization asks not which values work but which working value is largest or smallest, and its answer is a single number. One variable comes first.

Problem
A number xx satisfies 6x+11≤956x+11≤95. Solve for the bound the 8.3 way, then check the bound itself is allowed. Enter the largest value xx can take.
Show a hint
  • Subtract 1111 from both sides, then divide by the positive 66. That gives a ceiling on xx, a number xx cannot exceed.
  • The ceiling is the answer only if xx can equal it. Put the ceiling back into 6x+11≤956x+11≤95 and see whether the inequality still holds.
Show the full solution
Subtracting 1111 and dividing by 66 gives x≤14x≤14, and x=14x=14 gives 6(14)+11=956(14)+11=95, which is allowed, so the largest value is 1414​. The bound alone was not enough. The check that 1414 is itself allowed is the second half of the answer, and the next problem shows why it can fail.
Problem
Two numbers xx and yy satisfy x+y≤24x+y≤24 and y≥7y≥7. It is tempting to say xx can reach 2424. Decide whether it actually can, then enter the largest value xx can take.
Show a hint
  • Reaching x=24x=24 forces y≤0y≤0. Check whether the constraint on yy allows that.
  • Rewrite the first constraint as x≤24−yx≤24−y, then make yy as small as the second constraint permits.
Show the full solution
Since x≤24−yx≤24−y and yy is at least 77, x≤17x≤17, and x=17x=17, y=7y=7 satisfies both constraints, so the largest value is 1717​. The bound 2424 fails because no allowed pair reaches it. A bound nothing reaches is not a maximum.
Key idea
A maximum is proved in two parts, a bound and a case that reaches it. A bound like x≤24x≤24 says only that nothing allowed beats 2424. It does not say 2424 is allowed. The last problem's bound failed exactly there. No allowed pair reaches 2424, so the true maximum is 1717, not 2424. A bound together with one allowed value equal to it is the two-part answer, every maximum in this lesson needs both halves, and a minimum needs the mirror image, a floor and a case that reaches the floor.
Problem
Markers cost 6 dollars each and Lena has 80 dollars to spend on them and nothing else. Enter the largest number of markers she can buy.
Show a hint
  • Write the constraint as 6n≤806n≤80 and solve for nn. The bound you get is not a whole number.
  • A count of markers must be a whole number. Step down to the nearest whole number and check that its cost fits inside the 80 dollars.
Show the full solution
From 6n≤806n≤80, n≤1313n≤1331​, and since markers come in whole numbers the most is 1313, costing 7878 dollars, so the answer is 1313​. The bound 13131331​ is not a possible count, since counts are whole numbers, and among whole numbers nothing larger than 1313 stays within the 8080 dollars.
Problem
A number xx satisfies all three of 2x≤302x≤30, x+8≤20x+8≤20 and 4x≤504x≤50. Each constraint alone caps xx. Enter the largest value xx can take.
Show a hint
  • Solve each of the three inequalities separately. You get three different ceilings on the same xx.
  • xx has to obey all three at once, so only the lowest of the three ceilings can be reached. Check that value against the other two constraints.
Show the full solution
The three constraints cap xx at 1515, 1212, and 12121221​, and every allowed value must sit under all three, so the largest is the smallest cap, 1212​. The cap 12121221​ is close but looser. Only the tightest cap binds, and 1212 passes the other two checks.
Key idea
When several constraints cap the same quantity, the smallest cap binds. An allowed value satisfies every constraint at once, so it sits at or below each cap, and in particular at or below the smallest. The smallest cap itself satisfies the looser constraints automatically, so it is reached, and it is the maximum. The constraint whose cap is the answer is called binding, the others are called slack, and the reached half still gets checked against every constraint, not just the binding one.

With two variables the allowed values are no longer a stretch of the number line but one of 8.4's regions. Its corners sit where boundary lines cross, found by solving the pair as a system, chapter 5's work. A crossing counts as a corner only when it also satisfies every other constraint, since a point outside the region is not a corner of it.

Problem
One corner of a region is the point where the boundary lines 2x+y=252x+y=25 and x+3y=30x+3y=30 cross. Solve the system and enter the xx-coordinate of that corner.
Show a hint
  • A corner is just where two boundary lines meet, the system-solving from chapter 5. Solve the first equation for yy to set up a substitution.
  • Substituting y=25−2xy=25−2x into x+3y=30x+3y=30 leaves one equation in xx. Solve it, then check the pair in both boundary equations.
Show the full solution
Substituting y=25−2xy=25−2x into x+3y=30x+3y=30 gives −5x=−45−5x=−45, so the corner is (9,7)(9,7) and the xx-coordinate is 99​. Nothing new happened here. Finding a corner is exactly the line-crossing work of chapters 5 and 7.
Problem
The points satisfying x≥0x≥0, y≥0y≥0, x+y≤10x+y≤10 and 3x+y≤183x+y≤18 form a region. Enter how many corners this region has.
Show a hint
  • Cross the boundary lines in pairs, but keep only the crossings that satisfy every other constraint. Some crossings land outside the region.
  • Where x+y=10x+y=10 meets the xx-axis, check whether 3x+y≤183x+y≤18 still holds. A sketch the 8.4 way settles the count if it is unclear.
Show the full solution
The crossings that satisfy all four constraints are (0,0)(0,0), (6,0)(6,0), (4,6)(4,6) and (0,10)(0,10), so the number of corners is 44​. The crossings (10,0)(10,0) and (0,18)(0,18) each fail the constraint they do not sit on. A crossing outside the region is not a corner of it.
Key idea
On a region cut out by linear constraints, a linear expression takes its largest and smallest values at corners. That is the corner fact. Along any one edge the expression changes steadily in one direction, or not at all, so a point in the middle of an edge never beats both of its ends. Walking to the better end, then along the next edge, only ever stops at a corner. So however many points the region contains, and it contains infinitely many, only the corners need checking.

The whole method fits in one pass. List the constraints, find every corner by crossing boundary pairs and keeping the crossings that satisfy everything else, evaluate the expression at each corner, and take the best. The winning value occurs at an actual point of the region, so both halves of the two-part answer are settled at once.

Problem
A region has corners (0,0)(0,0), (8,0)(8,0), (6,4)(6,4) and (0,7)(0,7). Evaluate 3x+2y3x+2y at all four corners and enter the largest value it takes on the region.
Show a hint
  • There is one evaluation per corner, four in all. Skipping any of them risks missing the largest value.
  • At (8,0)(8,0) the yy term is zero. Compare that corner against (6,4)(6,4), where both terms are positive.
Show the full solution
The corner values are 00, 2424, 2626 and 1414, so the largest value of 3x+2y3x+2y on the region is 2626​. At (8,0)(8,0) the value is 2424, two less than at (6,4)(6,4), which is why every corner needs to be checked.
Fun fact
In 1939 George Dantzig arrived late to a statistics class and copied two problems off the board, taking them for homework. He handed in solutions days later. They were not homework, they were open problems nobody had solved.
Problem
The constraints x≥2x≥2, y≥1y≥1 and x+y≤9x+y≤9 cut out a triangle. Find its corners and enter the smallest value 3x+4y3x+4y takes on the triangle.
Show a hint
  • The three corners come from crossing the boundaries in pairs, and two come cheap since two boundaries are the lines x=2x=2 and y=1y=1.
  • A minimum sits at a corner for the same edge reason a maximum does. Evaluate 3x+4y3x+4y at all three corners and keep the smallest value.
Show the full solution
The corners are (2,1)(2,1), (8,1)(8,1) and (2,7)(2,7), where 3x+4y3x+4y equals 1010, 2828 and 3434, so the smallest value is 1010​. Minimizing is the same table as maximizing. Only the end you read it from changes.
Key idea
The corner method. Cross the boundary lines in pairs, discard any crossing that violates another constraint, evaluate the expression at each surviving corner, and keep the best value. A minimum is the identical work with the smallest entry kept instead of the largest, because the corner fact of the last rule holds at both ends of the list, so one table of corner values answers both questions.

A corner can have fractional coordinates, but a count of objects must be whole. The value at such a corner is still a bound. Round the bound down, then find an allowed whole-number point that reaches it. Rounding the corner's coordinates instead can give a point outside the region or miss the best plan, and the next problem sets exactly that trap.

Problem
A snack stand makes xx fruit cups and yy lemonades, whole numbers of each. Supplies allow x+y≤8x+y≤8 and prep time allows 3x+y≤153x+y≤15. Each fruit cup earns 2 dollars and each lemonade 1 dollar. Enter the largest number of dollars the stand can earn.
Show a hint
  • Find the corners of the region and evaluate the earnings at each one. The best corner has fractional coordinates, so its value is only a bound, not yet the answer.
  • Round that bound down to a whole number of dollars, then find whole numbers of cups and lemonades that satisfy both constraints and earn exactly that amount.
Show the full solution
The best corner is (72,92)(27​,29​), where 2x+y=11122x+y=1121​, so earnings are at most 1111, and x=3x=3, y=5y=5 satisfies both constraints and earns 1111​. Rounding the corner's coordinates down to (3,4)(3,4) earns only 1010 and misses the best plan. Round the bound down, then look for an allowed point that reaches it.
Problem
Mara has 75 dollars to spend on cupcake boxes. Each box costs 8 dollars and holds 12 cupcakes, and her backpack has room for 60 cupcakes. Enter the largest number of boxes she can carry home.
Show a hint
  • Two constraints cap the number of boxes, one from the budget and one from the backpack. Work out both caps before trusting either.
  • Money allows 99 boxes, but 99 boxes hold 108108 cupcakes. Which cap is actually the smaller one?
Show the full solution
The budget allows 99 boxes but the backpack caps the count at 60÷12=560÷12=5, and the smaller cap is the real limit, so the most Mara can carry home is 55​. Money is the slack constraint here. The limit comes from whichever cap is smaller, not from whichever the problem states first.
Key idea
A whole-number answer is the corner bound rounded down, then checked. The corner value is a bound, not yet an answer. Round it down, then look for an allowed whole-number point that reaches it, checking every constraint, not only the one the bound came from. A bound with such a point is attainable. If no allowed point reaches the rounded bound, it is not, so step down one and check again. A smallest-count question is the mirror image. Its bound is rounded up, and the check is that one fewer falls short. Skipping that check is the one error this lesson exists to prevent.

The chapter comes together here. Each constraint is rearranged under 8.1's rules and solved into a bound the 8.3 way, the region and its corners are drawn the 8.4 way, and the best corner is picked out with this lesson's two-part answer. Two problems remain, and each uses all of it at once.

Problem
The constraints x≥0x≥0, y≥0y≥0, 3x+y≤213x+y≤21 and x+2y≤12x+2y≤12 cut out a four-cornered region. Find all four corners, evaluate 5x+4y5x+4y at each, and enter the largest value it takes.
Show a hint
  • Cross the boundary lines in pairs and discard any crossing that violates another constraint. Exactly four corners survive.
  • The corners on the axes come quickly. The last corner is where 3x+y=213x+y=21 meets x+2y=12x+2y=12, a chapter 5 system. Then evaluate 5x+4y5x+4y at all four.
Show the full solution
The corners are (0,0)(0,0), (7,0)(7,0), (6,3)(6,3) and (0,6)(0,6), since the crossings (12,0)(12,0) and (0,21)(0,21) each fail the constraint they do not sit on, and 5x+4y5x+4y takes the values 00, 3535, 4242 and 2424, so the largest value is 4242​. Evaluating at all four corners is the whole check, since the largest value must occur at one of them.
Problem
Whole numbers x≥0x≥0 and y≥0y≥0 satisfy 2x+y≤162x+y≤16 and x+3y≤21x+3y≤21. Enter the largest value the expression 7x+6y7x+6y can take over all such pairs.
Show a hint
  • Run the corner method to get the bound. The best corner is not a whole-number point, so the bound is not attained.
  • Fix xx at each whole value from 00 to 88, take the largest yy both constraints allow, and evaluate 7x+6y7x+6y. Keep the best of the nine columns.
Show the full solution
The best corner is (275,265)(527​,526​), where 7x+6y=697x+6y=69, so 6969 is a bound but no whole-number point reaches it, and scanning each column, xx from 00 to 88 with the largest allowed yy, finds the best allowed point (6,4)(6,4), where 7x+6y=667x+6y=66​. The scan misses nothing, since for each xx the expression is largest at the biggest allowed yy, and the best of the nine columns is 6666.

Every boundary in this chapter was a straight line because every expression was linear. Chapter 9 turns to expressions where a letter is multiplied by itself. Lesson 9.1 opens Quadratics I with factoring, writing x2+7x+12x2+7x+12 as (x+3)(x+4)(x+3)(x+4), two linear factors, so the straight-line work just finished stays in use.

Practice these ideas

Practice
Of all the numbers satisfying x+6≤25x+6≤25, enter the largest.
Show the solution
Subtracting 6 gives x≤19x≤19, and 19+6=2519+6=25 is allowed, so the largest is 1919​.
Practice
A number yy satisfies 5y+9≤1095y+9≤109. Solve, check the bound is allowed, and enter the largest value of yy.
Show the solution
5y≤1005y≤100 gives y≤20y≤20, and y=20y=20 gives exactly 109109, so the largest value is 2020​.
Practice
Erasers cost 4 dollars each and Ben has 35 dollars. Enter the largest number of erasers he can buy.
Show the solution
4n≤354n≤35 gives n≤834n≤843​, and erasers come whole, so Ben buys 88​. The check matters, 88 erasers cost 3232 dollars and a ninth would break the budget.
Practice
Enter the largest value of xx that satisfies −2x≥10−2x≥10.
Show the solution
Dividing by −2−2 flips the inequality to x≤−5x≤−5, and x=−5x=−5 gives exactly 1010, so the largest is −5−5​. The flip is 8.1's rule, and forgetting it points the ray the wrong way.
Practice
Enter the smallest number satisfying x−7≥52x−7≥25​, as an exact fraction or decimal.
Show the solution
Adding 7 gives x≥192x≥219​, and x=192x=219​ satisfies the original exactly, so the smallest value is 192219​​.
Practice
An integer nn satisfies 4n<664n<66. Enter the largest possible value of nn.
Show the solution
4n<664n<66 gives n<16.5n<16.5, and the largest integer below the cutoff is 1616​. The check 4⋅16=64<664⋅16=64<66 works, and the answer would be the same with ≤≤ since 16.5 is not an integer.
Practice
Raffle tickets cost 8 dollars each and a class must raise at least 210 dollars. Enter the smallest number of tickets that reaches the goal.
Show the solution
8n≥2108n≥210 gives n≥2614n≥2641​, and tickets come in whole numbers, so the smallest count that reaches the goal is 2727​. The bound is rounded up because it is not whole. Selling 26 raises only 208 dollars and misses the goal.
Practice
Candles cost 6 dollars each, the budget is 150 dollars, and the gift box holds three rows of seven candles. Enter the largest number of candles that can be bought and boxed.
Show the solution
Money allows 2525 candles but the box holds only 2121, and the smallest cap binds, so the answer is 2121​. The reached half still checks out, since 2121 candles cost 126126 dollars, inside the budget.
Practice
The boundary lines of x+y≤11x+y≤11 and 3x−y≤103x−y≤10 cross at a corner of the region where both hold. Enter the xx-coordinate of that corner, as an exact fraction or decimal.
Show the solution
Adding the boundary equations gives 4x=214x=21, so the corner has x=214x=421​​. Substituting back into x+y=11x+y=11 gives y=234y=423​, and a corner with fractional coordinates is nothing unusual.
Practice
How many corners does the region x≥0x≥0, y≥0y≥0, x+y≤6x+y≤6 have?
Show the solution
The three crossings (0,0)(0,0), (6,0)(6,0) and (0,6)(0,6) all lie in the region, so the count of corners is 33​.
Practice
A region has corners (0,0)(0,0), (7,0)(7,0), (5,6)(5,6) and (0,9)(0,9). Enter the largest value of 2x+3y2x+3y on the region.
Show the solution
The corner values are 00, 1414, 2828 and 2727, so the largest value is 2828​. The close second is (0,9)(0,9) with 2727, so the corner with the biggest yy coordinate is not the best one here.
Practice
A region has corners (3,7)(3,7), (6,4)(6,4) and (9,9)(9,9). Enter the smallest value of 3x+2y3x+2y on the region.
Show the solution
The corner values are 2323, 2626 and 4545, so the smallest value on the region is 2323​.
Practice
A region has corners (0,0)(0,0), (8,0)(8,0), (5,7)(5,7) and (0,9)(0,9). The expression 9x+4y9x+4y is largest at one corner. Enter that corner's yy-coordinate.
Show the solution
The corner values are 00, 7272, 7373 and 3636, so the largest is 7373, at (5,7)(5,7), and that corner's yy-coordinate is 77​. The question asks for the coordinate itself, not the value 7373.
Practice
The points satisfying x≥0x≥0, y≥0y≥0, x≤5x≤5, y≤5y≤5, x+y≥2x+y≥2 and x+y≤8x+y≤8 form a region. Enter how many corners it has.
Show the solution
The boundary passes through (2,0)(2,0), (5,0)(5,0), (5,3)(5,3), (3,5)(3,5), (0,5)(0,5) and (0,2)(0,2), so the count of corners is 66​. Cutting off a corner of the square trades one vertex for two, and that happens at both (0,0)(0,0) and (5,5)(5,5), so the square's four corners become six.
Practice
Find the corners of the region satisfying x≥0x≥0, y≥0y≥0, x+y≤10x+y≤10 and 4x+y≤254x+y≤25, then enter the largest value 3x+4y3x+4y takes on the region.
Show the solution
The corners are (0,0)(0,0), (254,0)(425​,0), (5,5)(5,5) and (0,10)(0,10), with values 00, 754475​, 3535 and 4040, so the largest is 4040​. The largest value occurs at an axis corner, not at the crossing of the two slanted lines.
Practice
Find the corners of the region satisfying x≥3x≥3, y≥2y≥2 and x+y≤12x+y≤12, then enter the smallest value of 6x+7y6x+7y on that region.
Show the solution
The corners are (3,2)(3,2), (10,2)(10,2) and (3,9)(3,9), with values 3232, 7474 and 8181, so the smallest value is 3232​.
Practice
Whole numbers x≥0x≥0 and y≥0y≥0 satisfy 3x+2y≤193x+2y≤19 and x+y≤7x+y≤7. Enter the largest value 4x+y4x+y can take.
Show the solution
The best corner (193,0)(319​,0) gives the bound 25132531​, no allowed whole-number pair gives a value of 2525, and at (6,0)(6,0) the value is 4⋅6+0=244⋅6+0=24​. This is the step-down case, where the rounded bound of 2525 has no reaching pair and the maximum is the next value an allowed pair reaches.
